meta.title: Who really said "The trouble with most people is that they think with their hopes or fears rather than with their minds"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No primary source ties this line to Will Durant. It lives only on quote sites and is absent from Wikiquote’s Durant page—an unsupported attribution.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The trouble with most people is that they think with their hopes or fears rather than with their minds'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Will Durant everywhere online, yet no book, essay, or speech is ever cited—and Wikiquote’s Durant page doesn’t list it. An unsupported attribution.

answer.label: Not verified as Will Durant’s
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Will Durant across quote sites, almost always in the fuller form “…their hopes or fears or wishes rather than with their minds.” But no book, essay, speech, or letter is ever cited, and it does not appear on Wikiquote’s extensive Durant page—not even among his misattributed lines. No primary Durant source could be found, so the attribution is unsupported; the true origin of the wording is unknown.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Quote-aggregator sites; no dated primary attestation

source.excerpt: The trouble with most people is that they think with their hopes or fears or wishes rather than with their minds.
trail: The quote is attributed to Will Durant on Goodreads, which carries no source and notes its quotes are “not verified.”
It is repeated with the same bare byline on BrainyQuote and other aggregators—never with a book, page, or date.
It does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Will Durant page, including its list of misattributed lines—a strong sign no primary source exists.
No Quote Investigator entry treats this line; its nearest study of a “rather die than think” quip is a different saying that never mentions Durant.
source.excerptNote: The most common circulating form includes “or wishes”; the shorter “hopes or fears” variant is a later trimming. Neither wording has been tied to a specific Durant text.

sourceLink.text: Will Durant on Wikiquote (this line is absent)

source.rightsNote: Because the exact wording cannot be tied to any specific published work—by Durant or anyone else—its first-publication date is unknown, so no copyright status can be asserted. It would be wrong to label an unsourced line “public domain.”

author.name: Will Durant
author.heading: About Will Durant
author.bio: Will Durant was an American writer and historian best known for The Story of Philosophy (1926) and, with his wife Ariel, the eleven-volume The Story of Civilization (1935–1975), for which they shared the 1968 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction. Durant received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1977. His accessible, aphoristic prose has made him a frequent magnet for polished sayings he never actually published.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest traceable attributions appear only on undated quote-aggregator websites (e.g., Goodreads, BrainyQuote), none citing a work by Will Durant.

misattribution.heading: An unsupported attribution
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet-name” quote: a tidy aphorism attached to a respected thinker to lend it authority, with no source ever supplied.

items.why: Every attribution traces to quote-aggregator sites—Goodreads, BrainyQuote and the like—none of which names a book, essay, speech, or page. The line is also missing from Wikiquote’s Durant page.

misattribution.truthLine: No documented Durant text has been found containing this sentence, and no other author has been identified as its source; until a primary citation surfaces, treat the wording as of unknown origin rather than genuinely Durant’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentiment—that people reason backward from what they wish were true—is a genuinely old one in the literature on rationalization and public opinion, which is likely why the crisp Durant-branded version spreads so easily. But an idea being in the air is not evidence that a particular person coined a particular sentence.

On a provenance site the distinction matters: this line is plausible-sounding and widely shared, yet it rests on nothing more than repetition. That is exactly the profile of a fabricated or drifting attribution, and it should be labeled as unverified rather than passed along as fact.
context.pull: Widely shared, endlessly attributed—and never once sourced.
